info.title: Project Atlas API
info.description: Cyber-physical monitoring platform. Assessment AT-26-L1-002. Every endpoint states the minimum role it requires; the check is enforced here, not in the interface.

get.description:
Public, and reports the dependency rather than just the process.

A health check that returns 200 because the web server is running tells
the operator nothing: the failure that matters is the database being
unreachable, and this service is useless in that state.

post.description:
Refresh tokens are single-use and rotated.

The reason is detection, not tidiness. If a refresh token is stolen, both
the attacker and the legitimate client eventually present the same token.
With rotation the second presentation is of an already-used token, which
cannot happen in normal operation - so it is treated as evidence of theft
and the whole token family for that user is revoked, forcing a re-login.

Revokes the presented refresh token.

The access token stays valid until it expires. This is stated rather than
papered over: a stateless token cannot be recalled, and pretending
otherwise would mean a revocation lookup on every request. The bound is
the fifteen-minute lifetime, which is why the lifetime is short.

get.description:
FR-01, FR-03. Deleted devices are excluded: `deleted_at` is a soft delete,
because telemetry rows carry a foreign key to the device and a hard delete
would either fail or take history with it.

schema.title: Response List Devices Api Devices Get

post.description:
FR-01, FR-19.

The secret is generated here, handed to the broker, returned once, and
never persisted by the platform. Report 8.7 puts device credential
material in the broker's own store precisely so that a stolen application
database yields no device credentials - the "credential theft from
database" row of the threat table depends on this being true in code.

delete.description: FR-02, FR-19. Soft delete; the broker client is removed for real.

patch.description:
FR-04, FR-19.

device_config is append-only: each change writes a new row rather than
updating one. The audit trail records what changed and who changed it; the
config history records what the device was actually told at each point in
time, which is what a reading from last Tuesday has to be interpreted
against. Those are two different questions and both get answered.

schema.title: Response List Thresholds Api Devices  Device Id  Thresholds Get

put.description:
FR-04, FR-19. This is the endpoint the FR-19 verification method names
directly: change a threshold, confirm previous and new values recorded.

get.description:
FR-13. Raw readings.

The index on (device_id, time DESC) created in 01_schema.sql is what makes
this cheap; the WHERE clause is ordered to use it, and TimescaleDB excludes
chunks outside the time range before reading any of them.

Response List Events Api Events Get

get.description:
FR-14. Defaults to active only, because the question a dashboard asks is
"what is wrong now", not "what has ever been wrong".

schema.title: Response List Alarms Api Alarms Get

post.description:
FR-14, FR-20.

Acknowledging is not clearing. The alarm stays raised until the condition
that raised it stops, which is the anomaly engine's decision, not the
operator's - report 10 makes clearing a function of the data. What the
operator asserts here is that a human has seen it. Conflating the two would
let an operator silence an active fault by pressing a button.

schema.title: Response List Users Api Users Get

post.description:
FR-23. The plaintext password exists only as a local variable for the
duration of the hash call. It is not logged, not audited, and not stored:
`audit.scrub` removes the key even if a future edit passes it in.

Deactivation rather than deletion: audit_log holds a foreign key to the
user, and deleting the account would either fail or orphan the record of
what that account did. FR-20 requires the second not to happen.

Refresh tokens are revoked in the same transaction. Without that, a
deactivated user keeps a working session for up to seven days; the
per-request active check in deps.py already covers the access token.

get.description: FR-19, FR-20. Read-only: there is no endpoint that writes or edits this.

schema.title: Response Read Audit Api Audit Get

DeviceRegistered.title: DeviceRegistered
DeviceRegistered.description:
The secret appears in this response and nowhere else, ever. It is not
stored by the platform in any form - report 8.7 places device credential
material in the broker, not the application database.
